claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has been reported in a hierarchical-heterostructured state with pronounced multilevel chemical fluctuations.

Adding imaging-derived mesoscale heterostructural descriptors to a machine-learning regression model will improve prediction of Young's modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness relative to conventional DFT/CALPHAD methods.
High-resolution TEM or SEM can be used to quantify phase distribution, local strain fields, and chemical short-range-order indicators for use as model descriptors.
Molar volume, elastic constants, and misfit volumes are relevant physics-based inputs for models of alloy strengthening and ductility.
Machine-learning methods can predict mechanical properties of single-phase and multiphase alloys with reasonable accuracy.
Spatial chemical fluctuations and local phase and interface characteristics mediate elastic and plastic deformation in hierarchical-heterostructured HfNbTiVAl10.
Explicit structural-heterogeneity descriptors enable a machine-learning model to correlate local microstructural features with global mechanical responses more effectively.
The hybrid model bypasses some computationally intensive DFT and CALPHAD calculations.
Toughness is sensitive to deformation and fracture-initiation sites.
Explicit DFT evaluation of alloy yield strength and fracture behavior is largely beyond currently available implementations.
First-principles simulations remain computationally challenging for disordered multi-principal-element alloys.
Standard DFT/CALPHAD approaches have limited predictive accuracy for fracture properties.
The proposed model will reduce RMSE for Young's modulus, yield strength, and toughness by approximately 20–30%.
The proposed model will be approximately ten times more computationally efficient than traditional DFT/CALPHAD methods.
Model reliability will diminish if relevant heterogeneities are not captured at sufficient imaging resolution.
Model reliability will diminish when the alloy morphology differs from the hierarchical heterostructures represented in the training data.
Predictions at very high strain rates or temperatures far from room temperature will lie outside the model's calibrated validity range.
Analogous machine-learning applications to high-entropy alloys provide a basis for expecting improved predictive performance.
